pages.title: Read the situation
pages.instruction: A claim being circulated. Read for the facts and the different priorities
pages.author: Neighbourhood post · simulated source
pages.subject: Permanent closure?
paragraphs: A neighbourhood post says a familiar café is closing permanently. It links to a photograph of a sign but does not name anyone from the business or reproduce the complete notice. Several replies repeat the permanent-closure claim and add assumptions about the staff and the reasons. None of those additions has a source in the material provided.

The post may alert readers to a real change, but it does not establish the duration or scope of that change. A responsible summary should not inherit every confident statement in the replies. Before forwarding it, compare the full notice and identify which details the business itself has actually confirmed.

pages.title: Read the situation
pages.instruction: The narrower notice. Read for the facts and the different priorities
pages.author: Café notice · simulated source
pages.subject: Service during renovation
paragraphs: The café’s notice says the dining area will close for renovation. Delivery will continue while work is carried out. It asks customers to follow the café’s own updates for changes in service. The excerpt does not say that the business is permanently closing and does not make claims about staffing.

This is a simulated notice for source-comparison practice, not a report about a real business. It is more directly connected to the service decision than the neighbourhood replies, but that does not justify adding a reopening date or an explanation that is absent. The practical distinction is between a closed dining area and an entirely closed business.

pages.title: Compare the examples
pages.instruction: A reporting structure must preserve attribution

rows.subject: Report with an identified source
rows.verb: It is reported that … / According to …
rows.example: According to the café’s notice, the dining area will close for renovation

rows.subject: A passive reporting structure
rows.example: The café is said to be closing — but who says so?

rows.subject: An earlier alleged event
rows.verb: is thought / reported to have + participle
rows.example: It was reported to have closed; the current notice does not support that claim

pages.instruction: Separate confirmed facts, unsupported claims and unknowns, then decide what to share

The earlier post’s claim of permanent closure is not supported by the official notice. Could you revise the update with that attribution intact?
pages.audioText: Hi, Ana. The source has clarified the café notice. The dining area is closing for renovation, and delivery will continue, but a reopening date has not been set. items.prompt: Which source should anchor the revised update?
items.answer: The revised update should be attributed to the café’s official notice
A reopening date has not been set

items.prompt: What is the useful next step for someone planning a visit?
items.answer: They should check the café’s own updates rather than repeat the unverified post

additionalAudios.audioText: Please don’t replace the false certainty with a confident reopening date. If people need to plan a visit, the useful next step is to check the café’s own updates rather than repeat the same unverified post. We can explain what the notice confirms and what it leaves open without implying that every part of the original rumour has been investigated independently.
